title: Priya and the Cake Catastrophe
markdown:
The Sugar Plum smelled of vanilla and impending ceremony. Priya the magpie stood on a stool, bright eyes alight, surveying a confection of spun-sugar roses and frosted ivy that reached skyward like a mountain with opinions.

“Aha!” she chirped. “The apex lacks definition!”

Benji, her fox brother, fur the hue of toasted hazelnut, sighed from a flour sack. “Priya. It is a cake. A most immense cake. Mrs. Gable is famously particular.” He knew his sister’s mind, where logic often soared on wings of more.

“Precisely! And I, a scholar of celestial alignment, shall bring that particularity to its harmonious conclusion!” Her wing blurred toward a spatula. Even grand structures, like constellations, needed one precise guiding touch.

A minuscule adjustment to a sugared peony at the very top. The bloom, once tilted, sat perfectly symmetrical. “See?” Triumphant tail-flick. “Geometry perfected. The essence of order.”

A tremor ran through the edifice. The balanced peony nudged a marzipan swan. Sugary neck trembling.

“Uh, Priya?” Benji ventured.

“Nonsense.” She dismissed him with a wing, gaze already on the ivy. The swan’s neck, too arched, received an elegant curve.

Suddenly grapes tumbled. A silver leaf whispered loose. The stately pyramid acquired a grander, almost ceremonial air. Roses leaned conspiratorially. Ivy swept with dramatic flair. Grapes gathered in an unplanned cluster at the base, like spontaneous offerings.

“It is opulent,” Benji murmured.

“Opulent is merely the precursor to sublime.” The edible gold leaf: too scattered. A swift flick. Gold clustered with more purpose.

Meanwhile, polite conversation at the entrance shifted. The first Horticultural Society members arrived. Eyes fell on the cake. A collective gasp — surprised admiration mixed with bewildered awe.

“Is it meant to be so architectural?” whispered a gentleman with a magnificent moustache.

“Positively ritualistic,” added a lady in a formidable hat.

Priya, oblivious, surveyed her handiwork. Magnificent. Yet a faint tremor tickled her wingtips. Less dessert. More monument.

Benji saw admiration morph into silent questioning. He trotted to her side.

“Priya,” calm, steady. “We sought a beautiful cake for a party. Not a centerpiece for a coronation.”

She blinked. Gaze from the impossible cake to her brother. The weight of engineered perfection finally landed. She had been aligning frosting with the heavens and had lost the simple purpose: smiles.

“Oh.” A small embarrassed chirp. “Yes. A party.”

Benji nudged her. “A magnificent cake it remains. The guests are here to enjoy themselves, not critique its structural integrity. Nobody panic. Quietly improve yourselves instead.”

Understanding passed. The cake was beautiful in its wildly extravagant way. It was also too much.

In a flash she began to unmake the excess. Ostentatious gold gathered into a modest saucer. Grapes redistributed into artful bowls at the base, no longer looking like tribute. Leaning roses coaxed into a convivial arrangement, as if they had always meant to gossip rather than preside. She left the peony — her first crime — only slightly less symmetrical than a star chart. Not the stark mathematical precision she had envisioned. Balanced. Inviting. A cake meant to be eaten. A party cake.

The guests, watching the subtle transformation, relaxed. A moustache that had been architectural settled into a smile. The formidable hat nodded, once, as if granting a truce. Tension went. They saw dessert, ready to be shared. Laughter bubbled. Sugar and vanilla filled the room with genuine warmth. Mrs. Gable, who had been hovering like a particular storm, allowed herself a slice of relief that did not require a speech.

Priya, no longer architect of excessive splendour, smiled at Benji. He winked. The gala took the cake in slices, and the peony, slightly less perfect than a star chart, was the first piece to go.
characters: Priya (a magpie astronomy volunteer), Benji (the fox younger brother)
